title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in North Korea: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in North Korea: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for North Korea: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) provides no accessible domestic civil-registry, healthcare, social-insurance, or probate portals to the public abroad, so this guide cites verified international statutory and treaty archives (WIPO Lex, FAOLEX, and HCCH) alongside official foreign consular health advisories and protecting-power contacts [1] [4] [5] [6]. Because remote digital administration is unavailable, residents and foreign families must coordinate directly in person through local People's Committees, assigned medical facilities, diplomatic missions, or protecting powers such as the Embassy of Sweden in Pyongyang [6] [8] [9].

steps.title: Assess medical care options and emergency evacuation
steps.html:
• Domestic constitutional entitlement versus practical hospital capacity: Under Article 72 of the Socialist Constitution of the DPRK, citizens hold constitutional rights to free medical care and state material assistance during illness, old age, or physical disability through public hospitals and local clinic districts [3] [4].
  • Foreign nationals and medical evacuation urgency: Official advisories from the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO Consular Advice) and Global Affairs Canada warn that hospital standards and clinical hygiene in North Korea are poor, anaesthetics and essential medicines may be unavailable, and medical evacuation insurance is essential for any serious or life-threatening condition [8] [9] [10].
  • Contact insurers and missions immediately: Where a foreign citizen requires urgent clinical transfer or medical evacuation, contact the travel or medical insurer, home-country consular crisis center, and (where applicable) the Embassy of Sweden in Pyongyang immediately [6] [9] [10].

steps.title: Clarify legal representation, guardianship, and consular access
steps.html:
• Consular protection limits for foreign citizens: Because the British Embassy in Pyongyang and several other foreign embassies remain closed, and DPRK authorities restrict consular access especially outside Pyongyang, families should contact home foreign ministries or Sweden (as Protecting Power for countries such as the US, Canada, and Australia) as soon as possible [6] [8] [9].
  • Statutory guardianship rules for foreigners: Under Articles 42 and 43 of the DPRK Law on External Civil Relations, guardianship normally follows the law of the ward's domicile, while DPRK law permits appointing a guardian inside North Korea if a foreign citizen residing or staying there lacks one [1] [2].
  • In-person local administration for residents: Within the DPRK, matters of incompetence certification and local administrative authority fall under competent DPRK organs and city or county People's Committees rather than remote electronic portals [1].

steps.title: Coordinate social support and cross-border home benefits
steps.html:
• Domestic disability and sickness assistance: For DPRK residents, workplace social insurance committees and local People's Committees process sick-leave, disability pensions, and state material support referenced in Article 72 of the Constitution [3] [4].
  • Home-country benefits for foreign nationals: Foreign families should preserve any medical summaries issued in Pyongyang for home-country disability insurance, employment leave, or social security claims once evacuation or return occurs [9] [10].

steps.title: Address wills and cross-border property rules early
steps.html:
• Governing law for wills and assets: Under Article 46 of the DPRK Law on External Civil Relations, a testament or revocation follows the testator's law of domicile and is treated as valid in form if it complies with DPRK law, the testator's country of residence, the place where executed, or the country where immovable property sits [1] [2].
  • Movable versus immovable assets: Under Article 45, immovable property follows the law of the country where the property is located, whereas movable assets follow domicile rules [1].
  • Execute outside-DPRK instruments under home law: Because local DPRK notarial access for foreign nationals is tightly restricted, executing powers of attorney and wills relating to external bank accounts or real estate under home-country law (where feasible outside North Korea or via accredited diplomatic channels) avoids severe bottlenecks [1] [8] [9].

steps.title: Plan for non-Apostille document authentication
steps.html:
• Consular legalization required: Per the HCCH status table, the DPRK is not a Contracting Party to the 1961 Hague Apostille Convention [5]. Any official medical, civil, or legal document issued inside North Korea for use abroad requires formal diplomatic or consular legalization rather than an Apostille [5] [8].
  • Maintain physical records and embassy contacts: Keep passport numbers, medical evacuation policy details, and contact details for the Embassy of Sweden in Pyongyang (+850 2 381 7910) or home foreign ministries readily accessible [6] [7] [9].
